summary: Mission Desk is a browser game where players design a space mission and a three-stage rocket. They choose a destination (Moon, asteroid Bennu, Mars or Jupiter and Europa), engines, propellant and science instruments. The game then checks the design against real physics: the rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ratio and Hohmann transfer orbits. A player learns why a mission fails, for example because it is short on Δv or overweight, and can fix the design within a $1500M budget. We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no extra libraries.
details:
What it does. Mission Desk teaches mission design through play. The player picks a destination and builds a three-stage launch vehicle by choosing the engine type, engine count and propellant mass for each stage. They then add instruments, each with its own mass, cost and science value.

How it works. Each stage’s Δv is calculated with Δv = Isp·g0·ln(m0/mf), including structural mass and engine mass. Thrust-to-weight ratio is checked at each stage ignition. Mission Δv comes from Hohmann transfer equations. The page shows the burn budget step by step (departure, then orbit insertion) and the transfer time. A mission succeeds only if it reaches orbit, completes the mission with 5% margin, stays in budget, and carries at least one instrument.

Benefits. Players learn mission trade-offs: more fuel adds Δv but also mass and cost, and efficient engines cost more.

Goals. Make orbital mechanics and mission planning easy to understand for students.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript only.

Limits. The model uses impulsive burns and circular, coplanar planet orbits, and a fixed ascent Δv of 9.4 km/s. It is a teaching model, not a flight-ready design.
